title: The DOM
summary: The DOM is the browser’s object version of a webpage, which JavaScript can inspect and update.

subtopics.title: Page object
subtopics.explanation: `document` represents the current page in the browser. Its methods let code find and create elements. It is like the front desk for the page’s tree of content. Code that runs before an element exists cannot find it, so load scripts at the right time or wait for the document structure. For example, use querySelector after the page element has been created.

subtopics.title: Find an element
subtopics.explanation: `querySelector` finds the first element matching a CSS selector, such as `#status` or `.menu`. It is like searching a map by a label. Check whether the result exists before using it because a selector may match nothing after the page changes. For example, check for a null result before adding a listener to a possibly absent element.

subtopics.title: Respond to events
subtopics.explanation: An event listener runs a function when something happens, such as a click or form submission. It is like a doorbell that calls someone when pressed. Attach listeners to the right element, and remove them when temporary components are discarded to prevent duplicate behavior or memory leaks. For example, listen for submit on a form and prevent the default only when JavaScript handles it.

subtopics.title: Update text
subtopics.explanation: `textContent` changes an element’s text without interpreting it as HTML. It is like writing a note onto a sign rather than asking the browser to parse new markup. Prefer it for user-provided text. If rich HTML is truly required, use a vetted sanitizer and a clear security boundary. For example, set textContent for a user-entered status message.

subtopics.title: Use safely
subtopics.explanation: Do not insert untrusted strings as HTML with APIs such as `innerHTML`. A malicious string could create scriptable markup or deceptive content. It is like allowing a visitor to rewrite a public notice. Use safe text APIs and validate data before building interactive content. For example, remove listeners when temporary UI is discarded to avoid duplicate actions.

foundations.overview: The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the browser’s live tree of elements for a web page. JavaScript can find those elements, respond to user actions, and update text or attributes. Think of it like a tree-shaped map of a document. Use it for interaction, but prefer framework state when a framework owns the interface and avoid treating untrusted text as HTML.
foundations.whyItMatters: The DOM connects JavaScript to browser content and interaction. Understanding when elements exist, how events fire, and how to update text safely is essential for reliable UI behavior.
foundations.browserPerspective: The parser builds the DOM as bytes arrive; it is a live structure the rendering engine reads to compute layout and paint. Mutating the DOM marks parts of the page dirty, triggering style recalculation, layout (reflow), and paint as needed.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Rendering a list of search results, toggling a menu open, validating a form and showing errors, updating a counter, and inserting content fetched from an API are all everyday DOM operations.
foundations.businessImpact: Smooth, correct DOM updates are the difference between a responsive product and a janky one; inefficient DOM work causes visible lag that frustrates users and hurts engagement.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding the DOM directly makes you better with frameworks, because you understand what they generate. It also explains performance patterns (batching, fragments) and security concerns (innerHTML/XSS).
foundations.performanceImpact: DOM reads and writes can be costly, and interleaving them or writing in tight loops forces repeated reflows. Batching updates and minimizing layout thrashing keeps the UI at 60fps.
commonUseCases: Selecting elements and updating their text or attributes
Building lists/cards from data by creating and appending nodes
Toggling visibility and styling via classList
Removing or replacing parts of the page in response to user actions

commonMisconceptions.myth: The DOM is just the HTML you wrote.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The DOM is a live in-memory tree the browser builds and that JS can change; it can differ from the original HTML source after edits.

commonMisconceptions.myth: innerHTML is the normal way to set text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Use textContent for plain/user text; innerHTML parses HTML and is an XSS risk with untrusted input.
It returns a static NodeList (not an Array); it does not auto-update, and you must spread it or use Array.from for array methods.

commonMisconceptions.myth: querySelector always finds an element if the selector is valid.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The selector may match nothing on this page or may run before the element exists.

commonMisconceptions.myth: innerHTML is safe when a string comes from a form.
commonMisconceptions.reality: User-controlled text can become executable markup; use textContent or sanitize trusted HTML.

steps.name: document
steps.detail: The root entry point; everything hangs off the document object.

steps.name: <html>
steps.detail: The root element node, with <head> and <body> as children.

steps.name: <body>
steps.detail: Holds the visible content elements, like <ul> and <li>.

steps.name: Element nodes
steps.detail: Each tag (<ul>, <li>) is an element node JavaScript can select and modify.

steps.name: Text nodes
steps.detail: The text inside an element ('New item') is its own child text node.

interactiveExamples.title: Select and change text
interactiveExamples.explanation: Grab an element with querySelector, then update its visible text with textContent. The page updates immediately. Open the preview to see the change.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The heading on the page reads 'Changed by JavaScript!'.

interactiveExamples.title: Build a list from data
interactiveExamples.explanation: Create nodes with createElement, set their text, and append them to a parent. Using a document fragment batches the inserts into a single reflow.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A bulleted list shows Apples, Bread, Milk; console logs 'items added: 3'.

codeLab.instructions: Implement togglePanel() so it shows/hides the #panel by toggling the 'hidden' class with classList, and updates the button's text to 'Show' or 'Hide'. The button should call togglePanel on click.
